name: Foxglove
lede: Foxglove is a medium purple named for the flower, though the books say more about the plant's role in green dyeing.

sections.title: The flower and the dye
sections.body:
The foxglove, *Digitalis purpurea*, was named "purple fingers" by the botanist Leonhard Fuchs, though St Clair says he never saw the plant that now bears his name [1]. The swatch here sits close to [[violet]] and [[lavender]] in the data.

As a dye plant it counts mostly for green. Pastoureau lists foxglove among the plant products used to dye cloth green in medieval Europe, and says none gave a pure, stable color [2]. St Clair also says foxglove and nettle can give green without mixing, though not the rich saturated green buyers wanted [3]. A different plant, Chinese foxglove (*Rehmannia glutinosa*), was the source of a reddish-yellow dye that Tang rules forbade common people and officials to wear [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: #745AA2 is a medium purple [9]. Field data for this swatch is as photographed on screens, not as seen in a garden [1][4]. The concordance of 29 color books finds only four strong mentions of this name, so the article stays short rather than pad the record [9]. Screen colors are approximate, and the swatch is a reference value, not a measured pigment [9].
